blocks.text: Let us trace the formula on a concrete grid until the arithmetic stops feeling abstract.
Laid out in row-major order, memory holds the eight values in this sequence:
The formula is `offset = r x 4 + c`.

items: `grid[1][0]` → 1 x 4 + 0 = **slot 4** → 50. First cell of row 1, right after row 0 ends.

blocks.text: Look at the third one. Moving from `grid[0][3]` to `grid[1][0]` — the end of one row to the start of the next — moves exactly one slot forward in memory. The rows are not separated by anything. The grid is a fiction we impose on an unbroken line.
The formula also runs in reverse. Given a slot number, integer division and remainder recover the coordinates:
This reverse direction is genuinely useful. It lets you loop once from 0 to R x C − 1 and derive the coordinates, instead of nesting two loops — a trick that appears in plenty of matrix problems.
